claim: REF 2c cells, when confined in circular mesoscale patterns (diameter = 344 µm) on rigid substrates, transition from spindle shapes to more compact morphologies over 48 hours.
source: We found that when REF 2c cells, a subclone of the REF52 cell line, were placed on circular micro-contact printed patterns (diameter = 344 µm), the boundary cells radially aligned over a period of 48 hr after cell seeding (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1C showing decreased elongation at 48 hr compared to 24 hr.

claim: REF 2c boundary cells align radially at 48 hours after seeding on circular patterns.
source: We found that when REF 2c cells, a subclone of the REF52 cell line, were placed on circular micro-contact printed patterns (diameter = 344 µm), the boundary cells radially aligned over a period of 48 hr after cell seeding (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly observed in phase contrast images and quantified in Figure 1B showing angle deviation measurements.

claim: The radial alignment of REF 2c boundary cells is not caused by oriented cell migration toward or away from the center.
source: Video tracking of individual inner and boundary cells showed that the radial alignment of boundary cells was not caused by oriented cell migration toward or away from the center (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—video 1), as most boundary cells stayed on the periphery of the pattern.
evidence: Supported by cell tracking data showing migration trajectories in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both innermost and boundary REF 2c cells migrated longer and faster between 24-36 hr than between 36-48 hr.
source: Moreover, both the innermost and boundary cells migrated longer and faster between 24 and 36 hr than 36 and 48 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C showing migration speed and length measurements.

claim: Reduced cell migration in REF 2c cells coincides with the formation of radial alignment at the pattern boundary.
source: This reduced cell migration coincided with the formation of radial alignment of cells on the pattern boundary.
evidence: Inferred from temporal correlation between reduced migration (36-48 hr) and radial alignment formation (48 hr).

claim: 3T3 fibroblasts maintain circumferential alignment on the boundary at both 24 and 48 hours.
source: In contrast, 3T3 fibroblasts maintained circumferential alignment on the boundary at both 24 and 48 hr (Figure 1A), consistent with previous reports.
evidence: Shown in phase contrast images in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: At 48 hr, REF 2c cells are more compact compared to 24 hr, and much more compact than 3T3 cells.
source: We found that at 48 hr, the REF 2c cells were more compact compared to 24 hr, and much more compact than 3T3 cells, as indicated by the smaller elongation parameter (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantified by elongation measurements shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: For REF 2c cells at 48 hr, boundary cells are significantly more aligned with the radial direction than inner cells.
source: Further, for REF 2c cells, the boundary cells were significantly more aligned with the radial direction than the inner cells at 48 hr, although these cells showed circumferential alignment similar to 3T3 cells at 24 hr (Figure 1B).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1B showing angle deviation as a function of distance from pattern center.

claim: REF 2c boundary cells are significantly more elongated than inner cells at 48 hr.
source: Boundary cells were also significantly more elongated and had a significantly larger cell area than inner cells (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1C showing elongation measurements.

claim: REF 2c boundary cells have a significantly larger cell area than inner cells at 48 hr.
source: Boundary cells were also significantly more elongated and had a significantly larger cell area than inner cells (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1D showing cell area measurements.

claim: 3T3 boundary cells are significantly more circumferentially aligned and elongated than inner cells.
source: The boundary 3T3 cells were significantly more circumferentially aligned and elongated than the inner cells but did not have any significant differences in cell area (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1B-D showing angle deviation, elongation, and area measurements.

claim: 3T3 boundary cells do not have significant differences in cell area compared to inner cells.
source: The boundary 3T3 cells were significantly more circumferentially aligned and elongated than the inner cells but did not have any significant differences in cell area (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1D showing no significant difference in cell area.

claim: The average tissue thickness of REF 2c cells increases slightly due to cell radial alignment.
source: Confocal fluorescence images of REF 2c cells stained with a cell membrane permeable dye CellTracker-Green suggested that the average tissue thickness increased slightly due to the cell radial alignment, while the boundary cells had a wedge-shape with a drastically reduced cell thickness on the pattern boundary side (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Shown in confocal images and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: REF 2c boundary cells have a wedge-shape with drastically reduced cell thickness on the pattern boundary side.
source: Confocal fluorescence images of REF 2c cells stained with a cell membrane permeable dye CellTracker-Green suggested that the average tissue thickness increased slightly due to the cell radial alignment, while the boundary cells had a wedge-shape with a drastically reduced cell thickness on the pattern boundary side (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Observed in confocal side view images in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The change in tissue thickness suggests cell volume conservation as the whole pattern condensed slightly while boundary cell area increased.
source: The change in tissue thickness suggests cell volume conservation as the whole pattern condensed slightly while boundary cell area increased.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of increased tissue thickness, decreased boundary cell thickness, and increased boundary cell area.

claim: On soft PMA substrates (E = 5 kPa), REF 2c cells become polarized at 48 hr and condense towards the center of patterns.
source: We found that on soft PMA substrates (E = 5 kPa, post height = 8.4 µm), REF 2c cells became polarized at 48 hr and condensed towards the center of patterns, resulting in reduced total cell area on each pattern.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 with actin staining and quantified total cell area measurements.

claim: On stiff PMA substrates (E = 1 MPa), the total cell area on each REF 2c pattern does not change between 4 and 48 hr.
source: On stiff PMA substrates (E = 1 MPa, post height = 0.7 µm), however, the total cell area on each pattern did not change between 4 and 48 hr, and only cells on the boundary became radially aligned, which is consistent with the results on flat PDMS substrates.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B showing no significant change in total cell area.

claim: On stiff PMA substrates (E = 1 MPa), only REF 2c cells on the boundary become radially aligned.
source: On stiff PMA substrates (E = 1 MPa, post height = 0.7 µm), however, the total cell area on each pattern did not change between 4 and 48 hr, and only cells on the boundary became radially aligned, which is consistent with the results on flat PDMS substrates.
evidence: Observed in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A showing actin staining patterns.

claim: REF 11b cells do not radially align at 48 hr on circular patterns.
source: We isolated and expanded several subclones of the REF cell line, and identified one subclone, named REF 11b, which did not radially align at 48 hr on circular patterns (Figure 2A).
evidence: Shown in phase contrast images and angle deviation quantification in Figure 2A.

claim: RNA-seq data revealed that a small subset of genes were expressed significantly differently between REF 11b and REF 2c subclones.
source: RNA-seq data revealed that while most genes have similar expression levels in REF 11b and REF 2c subclones, a small subset of genes were expressed significantly differently (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in RNA-seq data table in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some genes differentially expressed between REF 11b and REF 2c are associated with cell-substrate adhesion and contraction.
source: As some of these genes are associated with cell-substrate adhesion and contraction (e.g. INTEGRIN α7 and α8, MYL9, and COL16A1), we then measured the cell contractility of these two subclones.
evidence: Inferred from known functions of identified genes (INTEGRIN α7 and α8, MYL9, and COL16A1).

claim: REF 11b cells are significantly less contractile than REF 2c cells for both total force and force per area.
source: Traction force measurements for single cells of REF 2c and 11b showed that for both total force and force per area, REF 11b cells were significantly less contractile than REF 2c cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantified by traction force microscopy measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment with Blebbistatin prevents radial alignment of REF 2c boundary cells.
source: The boundary cells of the Blebbistatin and Y27632-treated groups were not significantly more radially aligned than the inner cells, compared to the vehicle control group with DMSO (Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown in phase contrast images and angle deviation quantification in Figure 2C.

claim: Treatment with Y27632 prevents radial alignment of REF 2c boundary cells.
source: The boundary cells of the Blebbistatin and Y27632-treated groups were not significantly more radially aligned than the inner cells, compared to the vehicle control group with DMSO (Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown in phase contrast images and angle deviation quantification in Figure 2C.

claim: Cell contractility is required for radial alignment formation in REF 2c cells.
source: These results suggest that cell contractility is required for radial alignment formation.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that inhibiting contractility with Blebbistatin and Y27632 prevents radial alignment.

claim: REF 2c and REF 11b cells have cadherin-mediated cell-cell interactions.
source: Staining with β-catenin suggested that there were cadherin-mediated cell-cell interactions among REF 2c and REF 11b cells while overlapping and empty spaces could be found among 3T3 cells without clear cell-cell junctions (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by β-catenin immunofluorescence staining in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: 3T3 cells have overlapping and empty spaces without clear cell-cell junctions.
source: Staining with β-catenin suggested that there were cadherin-mediated cell-cell interactions among REF 2c and REF 11b cells while overlapping and empty spaces could be found among 3T3 cells without clear cell-cell junctions (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by β-catenin immunofluorescence staining in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment with EGTA causes REF 2c boundary cells to be significantly more circumferentially aligned than inner cells.
source: We found that when treated with EGTA, the boundary cells were significantly more circumferentially aligned than the inner cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: Shown in phase contrast and fluorescence images with angle deviation quantification in Figure 2E.

claim: EGTA treatment does not significantly affect cell-substrate interactions in REF 2c cells.
source: To confirm that EGTA treatment did not significantly affect cell substrates interactions, we measured the contractility of single cells using the PMAs. As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3, EGTA treatment did not change the total traction force per cell or per cell area, suggesting calmodulin-mediated contractility does not predominate this system.
evidence: Quantified by traction force measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cell contractility and cell-cell adhesion are two essential factors required for the establishment of radial alignment of patterned REF 2c cells.
source: Together, we identify that cell contractility and cell-cell adhesion are two essential factors required for the establishment of radial alignment of patterned cells.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that inhibiting either contractility or cell-cell adhesion prevents radial alignment.

claim: REF 2c cells form aggregates on soft substrates and show similar tendency on rigid substrates reflected by radial alignment.
source: Importantly, REF 2c cells form aggregates on soft substrates and show similar tendency on rigid substrates (reflected by the radial alignment).
evidence: Observed from experiments on soft PMA substrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and radial alignment on rigid substrates (Figure 1A).

claim: The collective cell behavior of REF 2c cells is defined as 'condensation tendency', which requires both cell contractility and cell-cell adhesion.
source: We define this collective cell behavior as 'condensation tendency', which requires both cell contractility and cell-cell adhesion.
evidence: Defined based on experimental observations and requirements identified through drug treatments.

claim: Cell proliferation is not required for the formation of cell radial alignment in REF 2c cells.
source: Thus, we believe that the cell proliferation mediated remodeling is unimportant for the formation of cell radial alignment.
evidence: Supported by experiments with aphidicolin treatment showing radial alignment persists without cell proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).

claim: With aphidicolin treatment, REF 2c cell number does not increase significantly from 24 to 48 hr.
source: We found that with aphidicolin treatment, the cell number did not increase significantly from 24 to 48 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B showing cell numbers per pattern.

claim: With aphidicolin treatment, REF 2c cells still show radial alignment of boundary cells comparable to untreated controls.
source: In this condition, we still observed the radial alignment of boundary cells, which is quantitatively comparable with untreated controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C showing angle deviation measurements.

claim: A decrease in actin intensity occurs near the boundary of patterns for REF 2c cells, in the same location as the transition between isotropically oriented inner cells and radially aligned boundary cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found a decrease in actin intensity occurred near the boundary of patterns for REF 2c cells, in the same location as the transition between isotropically oriented inner cells and radially aligned boundary cells. (Figure 3).
evidence: Shown in fluorescence images and intensity plots in Figure 3.

claim: The actin intensity in the outmost layer of REF 2c cells is significantly lower than that of the inner cells.
source: Our Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) results clearly demonstrated that the actin intensity in the outmost layer was significantly lower than that of the inner cells.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing actin intensity as a function of distance.

claim: The actin intensity gradient in REF 2c cells is not simply a result of cell density differences.
source: To exclude the possibility that such actin intensity gradient is simply a result of cell density difference, we also quantified the total actin intensity and actin intensity per cell in inner cells and the outmost boundary cells. Consistently, a significant difference was found between inner and boundary cells, suggesting this actin intensity gradient was not simply a result of cell density differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C showing actin intensity per cell measurements.

claim: For REF 11b, there is a continued decrease in actin intensity from the center of the pattern to the outermost edge.
source: In contrast, for REF 11b, there was a continued decrease in intensity from the center of the pattern to the outermost edge (Figure 3).
evidence: Shown in actin intensity plots in Figure 3.

claim: 3T3 cells show no actin gradient.
source: This is in sharp contrast to the actin distribution of 3T3 cells, in which no actin gradient was identified (Figure 3).
evidence: Shown in actin intensity plots in Figure 3.

claim: Increasing steepness of the actin gradient negatively correlates with boundary cell angle deviation in REF 2c cells.
source: Our results showed that increasing steepness of the actin gradient negatively correlates with boundary cell angle deviation (r = − 0.533), suggesting actin gradient may contribute to the boundary cell radial alignment.
evidence: Shown in correlation analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B with Pearson correlation coefficient r = -0.533.

claim: The p-myosin distribution in REF 2c cells is almost uniform across the whole pattern, with only a small increase near the pattern boundary.
source: It was found that unlike actin distributions, the p-myosin distribution was almost uniform across the whole pattern, with only a small increase near the pattern boundary (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Shown in p-myosin immunofluorescence images and intensity plots in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The stiffness of REF 2c cells is isotropic.
source: Given the actin orientation being neither radially nor circumferentially aligned (see Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Materials and methods), we assume that the stiffness of the cells is isotropic.
evidence: Inferred from actin fiber orientation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the radial-alignment case from the Voronoi-cell model, boundary cells are larger in size and more elongated.
source: Our shape analysis shows that in the radial-alignment case, the boundary cells are larger in size and more elongated (Figure 4B), consistent with the experiments (see Figure 1C,D, REF 2c cells).
evidence: Shown in modeling results in Figure 4B and consistent with experimental data in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The Voronoi-cell model explains the cell morphology observed in REF 11b cells, where no radial alignment is observed without contractility.
source: The results also explain the cell morphology observed in REF 11b cells, where no radial alignment is observed without contractility (see Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, top rows).
evidence: Shown in modeling results in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A compared to experimental observations.

claim: The slight elevation of p-myosin in the boundary cells is not the cause of the radial alignment.
source: This suggests that the slight elevation of p-myosin in the boundary cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) is not the cause of the radial alignment.
evidence: Inferred from modeling results showing that contractility differential alone does not produce radial alignment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: Compared to inner cells, REF 2c boundary cells are under more significant and anisotropic strains but more minor tensile stresses on average.
source: The stress and strain analysis on individual cells from simulations show that the boundary cells and the inner cells are under different mechanical cues (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). Compared to the inner cells, the boundary cells are under more significant and anisotropic strains but more minor tensile stresses, on average.
evidence: Shown in modeling results in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The distribution of vinculin in REF 2c cells is uniform across the pattern area, except for reduced vinculin intensity near the pattern boundary.
source: However, we found that the distribution of vinculin was uniform across the pattern area, except for reduced vinculin intensity near the pattern boundary.
evidence: Shown in vinculin immunofluorescence images and intensity plots in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The overall vinculin intensity per cell in the outmost layer of REF 2c cells is comparable with inner cells.
source: The overall vinculin intensity per cell in the outmost layer of cells was still comparable with inner cells.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 4D showing no significant difference.

claim: Most REF 2c cells express nuclear YAP, which is independent of confinement and cell alignment status.
source: We also found that most of the REF 2c cells expressed nuclear YAP, which is independent of confinement and cell alignment status (24 hr vs. 48 hr).
evidence: Shown in YAP immunofluorescence images in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Local activation of mechanotransduction pathways mediated by vinculin and YAP in boundary cells is unlikely the cause for cell radial alignment.
source: These results suggest local activation of these mechanotransduction pathways in boundary cells is unlikely the cause for cell radial alignment, although we cannot rule out the involvement of other mechanotransduction pathways, such as those mediated by mechanosensitive ion channels and certain G protein coupled-receptors (Martino et al., 2018; Holle and Engler, 2011; Marullo et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from uniform distribution of vinculin and YAP, with acknowledgment of other possible pathways.

claim: Condensation tendency with stiffness differential near the pattern boundary is sufficient to replicate the radial alignment and increased elongation and area of boundary cells compared to inner cells in REF 2c in vitro.
source: In summary, we have shown that condensation tendency with stiffness differential near the pattern boundary is sufficient to replicate the radial alignment and increased elongation and area of the boundary cells compared to inner cells in the REF 2c in vitro.
evidence: Demonstrated through Voronoi-cell modeling results matching experimental observations.

claim: Both REF 2c and 11b cultured on ring patterns robustly show an actin intensity gradient from the center to the boundary, regardless of the change of topology and the radius of the inner boundary.
source: We found that surprisingly, both REF 2c and 11b cultured on ring patterns robustly showed an actin intensity gradient from the center to the boundary, regardless of the change of topology and the radius of the inner boundary.
evidence: Shown in actin intensity plots for ring patterns in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: 3T3 cells do not have an actin gradient for any ring patterns.
source: In contrast, 3T3 cells did not have an actin gradient for any ring patterns (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Shown in actin intensity plots for ring patterns in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: For both thick and thin ring patterns, the outermost boundary REF 2c cells radially align, but not REF 11b cells or 3T3 cells.
source: We found that for both thick and thin ring patterns, the outermost boundary REF 2c cells radially aligned, but not REF 11b cells or 3T3 cells, which are quantified using angle deviation (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Shown in phase contrast images and angle deviation quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: The innermost boundary REF 2c cells on ring patterns align circumferentially along the inner boundary.
source: Interestingly, the innermost boundary cells aligned circumferentially along the inner boundary.
evidence: Observed in ring pattern experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: The cell area increases significantly near the exterior pattern boundary for REF 2c on ring patterns.
source: The cell area increased significantly near the exterior pattern boundary for REF 2c (Figure 4—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 9 showing cell area as a function of distance.

claim: REF cells express a significant level of intercellular adhesion molecules like N-cadherin and β-catenin.
source: Unlike 3T3 fibroblasts, REF cells express a significant level of cell adhesion molecules, such as N-cadherin and β-catenin (Mary et al., 2002), and have isotropic actin meshwork in contrast to cortically distributed actin in epithelial cells.
evidence: Cited from previous literature (Mary et al., 2002) and confirmed by β-catenin staining in Figure 2D.

claim: REF cells have isotropic actin meshwork in contrast to cortically distributed actin in epithelial cells.
source: Unlike 3T3 fibroblasts, REF cells express a significant level of cell adhesion molecules, such as N-cadherin and β-catenin (Mary et al., 2002), and have isotropic actin meshwork in contrast to cortically distributed actin in epithelial cells.
evidence: Shown in actin staining images in Figure 3 and fiber orientation analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The condensation tendency of REF cells is similar to the 'active dewetting' process in MDA-MB-231 cells with inducible E-cadherin.
source: Notably, such condensation tendency is similar to the recently discovered 'active dewetting' process in a monolayer of MDA-MB-231 cells with inducible E-cadherin, where cell contractility and intercellular adhesion drive the retraction of the tissue monolayer (Pérez-González et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparison to previously published work on active dewetting.

claim: When confined in circular mesoscale patterns on rigid substrates, boundary REF cells can robustly develop radial alignment in mechanical equilibrium.
source: New to the active dewetting process, we show that when confined in circular mesoscale patterns on rigid substrates, the boundary REF cells can robustly develop radial alignment in mechanical equilibrium.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental observations in Figure 1 and modeling in Figure 4.

claim: The condensation tendency, together with an autonomously established tissue-scale actin gradient, are sufficient to explain the observed radial alignment in confined circular geometries.
source: By developing a Voronoi cell model (Bi et al., 2016; Olaranont, 2019), we discover that such condensation tendency, together with an autonomously established tissue-scale actin gradient, are sufficient to explain the observed radial alignment in confined circular geometries.
evidence: Demonstrated through Voronoi-cell modeling results in Figure 4.

claim: The distinct behavior of REF-like cells may play a functional role in collective migration and mesenchymal condensation.
source: The distinct behavior of REF-like cells may play a functional role in the collective migration and mesenchymal condensation, which are conventionally considered driven by chemotaxis (Takebe et al., 2015; Szabó and Mayor, 2018).
evidence: Speculative inference about potential biological function based on observed behavior.

claim: Actin intensity is proportional to local cell stiffness.
source: On the other hand, the actin gradient decreasing towards the boundary (Figure 3) suggests that there is a stiffness differential between the inner and boundary cells, given it is well-documented that actin intensity is proportional to the local cell stiffness (Tavares et al., 2017; Rotsch and Radmacher, 2000; Nawaz et al., 2012; Gavara and Chadwick, 2016).
evidence: Cited from established literature on the relationship between actin and stiffness.

claim: Epithelial cells, when confined in circular patterns, form nematic symmetry similar to 3T3 cells.
source: Epithelial cells, when confined in circular patterns, form nematic symmetry that is similar to 3T3 cells (Saw et al., 2017; Doxzen et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous literature on epithelial cell behavior.

claim: When epithelial cells are confined in ring-shape patterns, chiral spiral defects can be found.
source: However, when they are confined in ring-shape patterns, chiral spiral defects can be found (Wan et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from previous literature on epithelial cell behavior in ring patterns.

claim: The different cell alignment between epithelial cells and REF cells is likely due to the distribution of actin network.
source: The different cell alignment between epithelial cells and REF cells is likely due to the distribution of actin network.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of actin distributions between cell types.

claim: Actin is mainly distributed in the cell-cell junctions for epithelial cells.
source: It is well-known that actin is mainly distributed in the cell-cell junctions for epithelial cells (Fanning et al., 2012), while actin stress fibers can be found in REF cells even when they form a compact monolayer.
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about epithelial cell actin distribution.

claim: Actin stress fibers can be found in REF cells even when they form a compact monolayer.
source: It is well-known that actin is mainly distributed in the cell-cell junctions for epithelial cells (Fanning et al., 2012), while actin stress fibers can be found in REF cells even when they form a compact monolayer.
evidence: Observed in actin staining images in Figure 3.

claim: C2C12 myoblasts can self-organize into spiral patterns when confined using circular confinement.
source: Recently, Roux, Kruse, and colleagues reported that C2C12 myoblasts could self-organize into spiral patterns when confined using similar circular confinement (Blanch-Mercader et al., 2021a; Blanch-Mercader et al., 2021b; Guillamat et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from recent literature on C2C12 myoblast behavior.

claim: When cell proliferation is allowed in C2C12 myoblasts, the system continues to evolve to aster pattern with boundary cells elongated and radially aligned.
source: When cell proliferation is allowed, the system continues to evolve to aster pattern with boundary cells elongated and radially aligned (Blanch-Mercader et al., 2021b) and eventually out-of-plane mounds in pattern center (Guillamat et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from recent literature on C2C12 myoblast behavior.

claim: The formation of aster patterns in C2C12 cells is attributed to both directional traction forces and nematic active stresses.
source: Using hydrodynamic descriptions, they attributed the formation of such patterns to both directional traction forces and nematic active stresses (Blanch-Mercader et al., 2021a; Blanch-Mercader et al., 2021b).
evidence: Cited from recent literature on C2C12 myoblast modeling.

claim: Cell proliferation is a critical driving factor in aster pattern formation in the C2C12 system.
source: While cell proliferation is a critical driving factor in aster pattern formation in the C2C12 system, in our REF system, the stiffness differential is indispensable for the radial alignment formation.
evidence: Comparison to C2C12 system from literature and contrast with REF system findings.

claim: In the REF system, the stiffness differential is indispensable for radial alignment formation.
source: While cell proliferation is a critical driving factor in aster pattern formation in the C2C12 system, in our REF system, the stiffness differential is indispensable for the radial alignment formation.
evidence: Demonstrated through modeling results showing radial alignment requires stiffness differential (Figure 4).

claim: REF cells represent a unique class of cell systems that are different from typical spindle-like 3T3 cells, epithelial cells, and C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Together, the REF cells represented a unique class of cell systems that are different from typical spindle-like 3T3 cells, epithelial cells, and C2C12 myoblasts.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of REF cell behavior to other cell types throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neural crest cells migrate as a cohesive group mediated by self-secreted C3a.
source: Interestingly, neural crest cells migrate as a cohesive group mediated by self-secreted C3a (Carmona-Fontaine et al., 2011), and chondrocytes form mesenchymal condensation mediated by EGF signals (Qin and Beier, 2019).
evidence: Cited from literature on neural crest cell migration.

claim: Chondrocytes form mesenchymal condensation mediated by EGF signals.
source: Interestingly, neural crest cells migrate as a cohesive group mediated by self-secreted C3a (Carmona-Fontaine et al., 2011), and chondrocytes form mesenchymal condensation mediated by EGF signals (Qin and Beier, 2019).
evidence: Cited from literature on chondrocyte condensation.

claim: The condensation tendency of neural crest cells and chondrocytes may be relevant to their biological functions by facilitating their orientation towards the signal center.
source: The condensation tendency of these cells may be relevant to their biological functions by facilitating their orientation towards the signal center.
evidence: Speculative inference about potential biological function based on observed condensation tendency in REF cells.

claim: A positive correlation between actin and myosin spatial distributions has been widely reported previously.
source: A positive correlation between the actin and myosin spatial distributions has been widely reported previously (Martin et al., 2009; Banerjee et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from established literature on actin-myosin correlation.

claim: In the REF microtissue, the myosin gradient is not evident and does not coincide with the actin gradient.
source: However, in the REF microtissue, we have found that the myosin gradient is not evident and does not coincide with that of the actin gradient.
evidence: Shown in p-myosin staining in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 compared to actin staining in Figure 3.

claim: Myosin is associated with higher contractile force.
source: While it is well-documented that myosin is associated with higher contractile force (Murrell et al., 2015) and actin is associated with higher stiffness (Tavares et al., 2017; Rotsch and Radmacher, 2000; Nawaz et al., 2012; Gavara and Chadwick, 2016), in theory, we disentangled their roles in regulating the cell morphology at the REF tissue boundary.
evidence: Cited from established literature on myosin function.

claim: Actin is associated with higher stiffness.
source: While it is well-documented that myosin is associated with higher contractile force (Murrell et al., 2015) and actin is associated with higher stiffness (Tavares et al., 2017; Rotsch and Radmacher, 2000; Nawaz et al., 2012; Gavara and Chadwick, 2016), in theory, we disentangled their roles in regulating the cell morphology at the REF tissue boundary.
evidence: Cited from established literature on actin function.

claim: Differential stiffness with uniform contractility is sufficient to explain the radial-cell-alignment tissue boundary.
source: We reason that differential stiffness with uniform contractility is sufficient to explain the radial-cell-alignment tissue boundary.
evidence: Demonstrated through Voronoi-cell modeling results in Figure 4.

claim: The actin mesh architecture may affect the contractile machinery through the concentration of crosslinking proteins.
source: Indeed, the actin mesh architecture may also affect the contractile machinery, such as through the concentration of the crosslinking proteins (Kasza and Zallen, 2011).
evidence: Cited from literature on actin mesh effects on contractility.

claim: EGTA reduces cadherin-based cell-cell adhesion without significantly affecting cell adhesion to substrates.
source: To confirm this, we treated REF 2c cells with EGTA, which reduced cadherin-based cell-cell adhesion without significantly affecting cell adhesion to substrates (Pérez-González et al., 2019; Ohgushi et al., 2010; Rothen-Rutishauser et al., 2002; Al-Kilani et al., 2011; Koutsouki et al., 2005; Charrasse et al., 2002), at 24 hr and then examined the cell alignment at 48 hr.
evidence: Cited from multiple literature sources on EGTA effects and confirmed by traction force measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Blebbistatin inhibits myosin ATPase activity.
source: To verify that the cell contractility was required for radial alignment, we treated patterned REF 2c cells with Blebbistatin (to inhibit myosin ATPase activity) and Y27632 (to inhibit Rho kinase activity), drugs known to reduce cell contractility (Beningo et al., 2006), at 24 hr, and then imaged the patterned cells at 48 hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about Blebbistatin mechanism.

claim: Y27632 inhibits Rho kinase activity.
source: To verify that the cell contractility was required for radial alignment, we treated patterned REF 2c cells with Blebbistatin (to inhibit myosin ATPase activity) and Y27632 (to inhibit Rho kinase activity), drugs known to reduce cell contractility (Beningo et al., 2006), at 24 hr, and then imaged the patterned cells at 48 hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: Cited from established knowledge about Y27632 mechanism.

claim: Aphidicolin is an inhibitor of DNA replication.
source: To test this, we treated REF 2c cells with aphidicolin (1 µg/ml), an inhibitor of DNA replication (Ikegami et al., 1978).
evidence: Cited from literature on aphidicolin mechanism.

claim: REF-52 cell line stably expresses yellow fluorescent protein (YFP)-paxillin fusion protein.
source: Original Rat Embryo Fibroblast cell line (REF-52; RRID:CVCL_6848) stably expressing yellow fluorescent protein (YFP) - paxillin fusion protein is a gift from Dr. Jianping Fu.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods section describing cell culture.

claim: REF 11b and 2c subclones were generated by single-cell clone selection.
source: REF 11b and 2c subclones were generated by single-cell clone selection.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods section describing cell culture.

claim: The circular patterns used for cell confinement have a diameter of 344 µm.
source: We found that when REF 2c cells, a subclone of the REF52 cell line, were placed on circular micro-contact printed patterns (diameter = 344 µm), the boundary cells radially aligned over a period of 48 hr after cell seeding (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in Results section and Materials and methods.

claim: The ring patterns have an outer diameter of 400 µm and inner diameters of either 200 µm (thick ring) or 300 µm (thin ring).
source: To do so, we designed two ring patterns with different inner diameters (200 µm and 300 µm) and the same outer diameter (400 µm).
evidence: Stated in Results section and Materials and methods.

claim: The PDMS substrates used have a Young's modulus of 2.5 MPa.
source: As cells were patterned on PDMS substrates (Young's modulus E = 2.5 MPa), which are significantly stiffer than physiological extracellular matrices, we next tested whether a similar phenomenon could be observed on substrates with physiologically relevant stiffness.
evidence: Stated in Results section.

claim: Soft PMA substrates have an effective Young's modulus of 5 kPa with post height of 8.4 µm.
source: We found that on soft PMA substrates (E = 5 kPa, post height = 8.4 µm), REF 2c cells became polarized at 48 hr and condensed towards the center of patterns, resulting in reduced total cell area on each pattern.
evidence: Stated in Results section.

claim: Stiff PMA substrates have an effective Young's modulus of 1 MPa with post height of 0.7 µm.
source: On stiff PMA substrates (E = 1 MPa, post height = 0.7 µm), however, the total cell area on each pattern did not change between 4 and 48 hr, and only cells on the boundary became radially aligned, which is consistent with the results on flat PDMS substrates.
evidence: Stated in Results section.
